Agenda statement partial — 'I'll just take a few pieces of information down from you... and then we'll kind of go from there' names the what but never the how long (10-15 minutes)
No 'Sound good?' confirmation anywhere in the call
Special considerations never asked — no long walks, narrow hallways or tight turns at any of the three addresses
Storage cue dropped — customer said 'my cloth stuff like that I have in storage' and it was never probed as a possible stop
Access concerns never asked — no parking, driveway or truck-access probe, on a move with a straight-run staircase at the destination
No moving-stressors question
'Pricing is super simple' opener never used
Hourly rate stated inconsistently — quoted '$206' then corrected to '$208 is the, is the flat hourly rate' in the same breath, and no weekday/weekend tier framing
Meet Your Mover never described — no mention of the pre-move email with mover photo and info
'No hidden fees' stated generically ('there's no additional or hidden fees') but never itemized — no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees

No sense-check after the clock explanation ('Does that make sense?')
Walk distance never named as an estimate variable at any of the three stops
Save Your Ass prep speech essentially absent — no explicit prep-equals-shorter-move-equals-lower-bill framing, no consolidation examples (drawers, wall photos, toys, garden tools), no close
BOLDED key-details list at top of the email never mentioned
'Reply with any corrections' never asked — the verification ask was about whether the email arrived at both addresses, not whether the details were right
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' — the customer had to raise his own veteran-discount question unprompted

top_strength: Chauny handled a genuinely messy call structure — two quote scenarios, three addresses, a profile under someone else's email — without ever losing the thread, and she said so out loud when the customer offered to repeat himself: 'Or, or, nope I got every bit of it.' She then did the thing that actually sells a conditional quote: she priced both scenarios separately and showed her work. 'if we kept everything as-is, we did all of the stops... So your hourly rate is gonna be $206 that does include the two movers. The truck. It includes any kind of disassembling. And reassembling,' followed by the drop-the-second-stop version, 'three to four hours is what I'm Gran for that move if we don't have the 408. Which would still again the a cost estimate around let's just say $796 to 1002.' She also killed the trip fee confusion before it became an objection, confirming the $75 applies once either way. Her budget framing is a real strength: when the customer pushed back that the job would not take five and a half hours, she did not defend the range, she immediately re-priced downward — 'if for any reason it only takes, let's say three to four hours then you're only looking at about $693 to about $780 as the range... cause you only pay for the time used anyway.' The insurance explanation was the textbook version, with the competitor baseline attached: 'we do cover-up to $2,000 for any kind of incidentals. So which is much more than the standard 60¢ that our competitors offer.' And she has real warmth — the 'come on shiny. It's Friday. My, it's party mode' self-correction when she realized she had not asked the move date turned a mistake into a rapport moment, and the customer stayed with her for the whole 28 minutes.
coaching_note: The single highest-value fix is the Save Your Ass speech, because this specific call left money on the table with it. The customer volunteered the setup himself — 'All the little boxes and stuff... I'm just gonna put my truck. So really I just need help with a big stuff' — which is the carload tip, arriving from the customer instead of the rep. Chauny gestured at the idea once, 'if everything is ready to go and prepped like when we get there, we're just padding and getting it onto the truck then, yeah, you're only going to pay what you use,' but never made it a directive. On a job she quoted at 5.5-6.5 hours against a customer who thinks it is 3-4, the prep speech is the bridge between those two numbers: 'empty the dresser and nightstand drawers, pull the TVs off the stand and get the wall stuff down before we arrive — that is thirty to forty-five minutes straight off your bill.' She should also close two script gaps that cost nothing: Meet Your Mover never came up at all, and the email handoff stopped one sentence short. She said 'I'm going to send over a confirmation email to you just so you have that double-check make sure everything looks good' — but the only thing she actually asked him to verify was whether it arrived at both addresses. On a booking with three addresses, a date, a conditional stop and an email swap mid-call, the correction ask is not a formality, it is the accuracy control: 'read the bolded details at the top and reply if anything is off.' On tenure versus habit: the read here is tenure. Everything Chauny has clearly been trained on — the differentiators, No Worries with the 60¢ contrast, the On-Time Guarantee, no deposit, no cancellation fee, pay-on-completion, the lift gate upsell framed as a free benefit — she delivers naturally and unprompted. What is missing is not judgment or effort, it is script coverage she has not been handed yet: the agenda opener with a time box, the clock-starts-on-site line, the Save Your Ass block, Meet Your Mover, and the email verification ask. Those are five discrete sentences, not a behavior change, and they are worth roughly fifteen points. Three months in, that is a checklist problem, not a coaching problem.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely warm and human rather than scripted — she used 'Blake' four separate times, laughed at her own miss ('come on shiny. It's Friday. My, it's party mode'), complimented his furniture mid-quote ('these are some pretty good pieces, you know, the first location they don't make furniture like that'), and the customer stayed engaged and positive to the end, closing with 'sounds good I appreciate it. Thank you so much.'
